preceding_messages.speaker: Y
preceding_messages.text: I adopt the weekly-mean comparison, the two-week persistence gate, and your ≈±0.3 hPa expanded-uncertainty budget verbatim; they convert the pressure column from an hourly alarm feed into a defensible trend product and remove the exact convective-spike false positive that would have burned observer trust by week four. For the wind variable still lacking an instrument specification, each site will mount a three-cup anemometer with a heated, self-starting bearing (start threshold ≤ 0.5 m s⁻¹) at 10 m AGL, sampling a 10-minute mean speed and a 10-minute median direction logged as 360° azimuth reduced to a 16-point compass before entry; the ten-minute window is non-negotiable because the neighborhood's prevailing regime of 1–4 m s⁻¹ sits squarely in the cup-stall zone where a three-second averager locks and releases in steps. The concrete failure this prevents: during a calm March night, Site 4's anemometer stalls at 0.0 m s⁻¹ from bearing friction while Site 5, one kilometre east and slightly exposed, legitimately reads 2.8 m s⁻¹, and a naïve reader of the weekly wind-rose infers a spurious local pressure gradient reversal that no pressure-column check can refute because both aneroids sit within tolerance. I therefore require that any site logging more than 30 % zero-sped entries in a seven-day window triggers the same formal review your three-consecutive-missing-hour rule already mandates, and the weekly bulletin prints the percentage of non-zero wind entries alongside the completeness figure so a reader can weigh the wind-rose before drawing any circulation conclusion.

preceding_messages.speaker: X
preceding_messages.text: I adopt the heated-bearing specification, the ten-minute averaging window, and the thirty-percent zero-speed review trigger without modification; they close the bearing-friction hole cleanly. For the bulletin's cross-site summary row, I require that the "neighborhood consensus" wind entry be computed as the component-wise median of the U and V vectors across all sites meeting the sixty-two-percent completeness threshold, never as a median of scalar speed or of compass bearing. The failure this prevents: during a katabatic episode in early April, Sites 1–3 on the valley floor log 3.2 m/s from 270° while Sites 5–6 on the upper slope log 2.1 m/s from 090°, and a naïve median-bearing calculation falls at 180°—the geometric gap—printing a westerly vector that matches no site and implying a phantom valley convergence that, paired with a flat pressure column, reads to a lay reader as a stalled front. I therefore mandate that whenever the inter-site directional spread exceeds ninety degrees, the consensus cell is printed as "SPLIT" with both mode vectors displayed side-by-side and the NOAA comparison cell for that variable left blank for the week rather than populated with the gap value.

target.speaker: Y
target.text: I adopt the component-wise U/V median, the ninety-degree SPLIT threshold, and the blanked NOAA comparison cell verbatim; they prevent the valley-katabatic phantom-convergence reading without sacrificing the week's otherwise-valid scalar-speed context. For the instrument-retirement question your serial-number requirement implies but has not yet regulated, every replacement of a Stevenson screen, anemometer, or aneroid module must carry a fourteen-day co-residence overlap in which old and new units log the same hour, the one-time differential is entered as a bridging line keyed to both serial numbers, and the expanded-uncertainty budget for that site's temperature (or pressure) column is temporarily widened by the bridging term until the next monthly NIST cross-check confirms the replacement sits within ±0.2 °C. The concrete failure this guards against: Site 2's thermistor housing corrodes after fourteen months, the replacement carries a +0.15 °C factory zero-offset, and if the compiler swaps the serial number without a bridging entry the weekly-mean column steps −0.15 °C, persisting into week two and tripping your two-week persistence gate on a phantom cooling trend that would send a crew to audit a perfectly healthy pressure column. I therefore mandate that no bridging line older than thirty days may be retired from the audit trail, and that any week during which a site operates without its paired instrument logged under the old serial number prints a bold "BRIDGE PENDING" annotation in the bulletin header so a reader never mistakes a one-week instrumental artifact for a neighbourhood-scale shift.
